notes:
I couldn't find anything on netbible.org, bibleodyssey.org, oca.org or catholic.com, and nothing on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace readings of this chapter. Those are left out. Where a page labels a commentator's tradition, I say so. I haven't assigned traditions myself.

**v. 1**
- Timnah lay about four miles from Samson's home at Zorah, in Philistine territory. Pritchard says "went down" describes both the walk and Samson's spiritual decline. https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_14_commentary
- Wiersbe makes the same point: he left Israel's borders and fell for a heathen woman. https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_14_commentary
- Gill says Samson saw many women but singled this one out and fell in love at sight. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/judges/14-1.htm

**v. 2**
- Constable notes that "woman" comes first in the Hebrew sentence for emphasis: to Samson she was the ideal woman. Her appeal seems to have been her looks alone. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/judges-14.html
- Matthew Henry credits Samson for bringing his parents into it. In Henry's view, children shouldn't marry without their parents' advice and consent. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/judges/14-2.htm
- Barnes explains that the groom's parents arranged the match and paid the dowry to the bride's parents. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/judges/14-2.htm

**v. 3**
- Guzik: "she pleases me well" literally means "she is right in my eyes." Samson cared how things looked to him, not to the LORD. His demand ignored his parents and God's will (Deut. 7:3–4). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-14/
- Wiersbe links the phrase to the book's summary that everyone did what was right in their own eyes. https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_14_commentary
- Constable says "uncircumcised" marks her as someone outside faith in Yahweh. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/judges-14.html
- **Disagreement:** Henry thought it wasn't evil in itself to marry a Philistine. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jdg/Jdg_014.cfm
- Constable notes that the Law's explicit ban covered Canaanites, though the same reasoning applied to Philistines. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/judges-14.html
- The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary calls the marriage directly against God's law. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/judges-14.html

**v. 4** (the most debated verse)
- **Who is "he"?** The Hebrew just says "he." Bush, Keil and Fausset take it to mean Samson. Davis, Wood and Wiseman take it to mean God. https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_14_commentary
- The Pulpit Commentary also calls it doubtful. https://biblehub.com/judges/14-4.htm
- **Did God plant the desire, or allow it?**
  - Henry says the marriage was "of the Lord" in a strong sense: God put the choice into Samson's heart, not just overruled it afterwards. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jdg/Jdg_014.cfm
  - Jamieson-Fausset-Brown thinks the plan was probably prompted by the Spirit. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/judges/14-4.htm
  - Guzik says God did not make a reluctant Samson pursue her. God let him do what he wanted, though the act was sinful. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-14/
  - Constable says God permitted a marriage He didn't prefer. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/judges-14.html
  - Coffman says God didn't approve, but overruled Samson's stubbornness. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/judges/14-4.html
- Translation notes:
  - Ellicott says "occasion" is better rendered "a quarrel," and the Septuagint has "vengeance." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/judges/14-4.htm
  - Bush notes the Hebrew reads "from the Philistines," meaning the trouble would start on their side. https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_14_commentary

**v. 5**
- Guzik: Nazirites were to avoid all grape products, so being in the vineyards put Samson close to compromise. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-14/
- Coffman suggests there were several trips, and Samson moved ahead of his parents. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/judges-14.html
- Haydock (Catholic) explains that a "young lion" means one in full vigour. https://studylight.org/commentaries/hcc/judges-14.html

**v. 6**
- Constable: this is the first recorded show of Samson's strength. A lion leapt at Samson, but the Spirit leapt on him, probably showing that God could empower him against the Philistines. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/judges-14.html
- Trapp, quoted in the Preacher's Homiletical Commentary, says these surges came when God had work for him and did not stay with him permanently. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/judges/14-14.html
- Spurgeon praised Samson's modesty in not mentioning the lion. https://www.ccel.org/ccel/spurgeon/sermons29.vi.html

**v. 7**
- Constable: the Hebrew again means "right in Samson's eyes," making him typical of Israel in this period. Samson used God-given strength for his own ends. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/judges-14.html

**v. 8**
- Constable says bees don't normally live in carcasses, so this was a test of Samson's character. He quotes Emmrich, who reads the bees as a picture of Israel settling a land of idolaters. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/judges-14.html
- Henry says that by driving off the bees, Samson learned not to fear crowds of Philistines. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jdg/Jdg_014.cfm

**v. 9**
- **Did Samson break his vow?**
  - Guzik says yes: touching a carcass broke the Nazirite law (Num. 6:6–7), and he did it right after being filled with the Spirit. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-14/
  - Constable adds that Samson led his parents into defilement without their knowing. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/judges-14.html
  - Gill disagrees: Samson was an unusual Nazirite, and the law was relaxed for him, including the honey from the carcass. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/judges/14-19.htm
- **Christ-centred readings:**
  - Spurgeon saw in the scene a picture of Jesus, conqueror of death and hell, bringing sweetness to others. https://www.ccel.org/ccel/spurgeon/sermons29.vi.html
  - Guzik cites this but warns that no picture of Christ is perfect. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-14/

**v. 10**
- Guzik says the Hebrew means a "drinking feast," which put Samson's vow at risk. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-14/
- Constable thinks Samson probably drank wine there. He also notes the seven-day feast was held at the bride's home. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/judges-14.html

**v. 11**
- Henry says the thirty companions were sent to honour Samson as groomsmen. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/judges/14-19.html
- Constable says the bride's family seemed proud of him, and Samson fit comfortably into Philistine society. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/judges-14.html

**v. 12**
- Constable: riddles were common entertainment. The same Hebrew word is used for the Queen of Sheba's hard questions to Solomon. The "linen garments" were large wraps worn next to the skin, and the "clothes" were costly festive garments. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/judges-14.html

**v. 13**
- Precept Austin points out that the stakes were high. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/60757/

**v. 14**
- Guzik: Samson was morally weak but quick-witted. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-14/
- Biblehub's study notes see a picture of Christ, the Lion of Judah, as the source of sweetness. https://biblehub.com/judges/14-14.htm
- F.B. Meyer applies the young lion to the temptations that roar at believers. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/60757/

**v. 15**
- Constable: she is called "wife" before the marriage was consummated, which happened at the end of the feast. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/judges-14.html
- Guzik: she acted out of fear because of the threat, though Samson could easily have protected her. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-14/

**v. 16**
- Guzik says she manipulated Samson by making herself a burden. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-14/
- Constable finds Samson's loyalty to his parents understandable, since the marriage wasn't yet consummated. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/judges-14.html

**v. 17**
- Guzik: the strongest man was easily manipulated, and this weakness would later bring him down. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-14/
- Constable says she passed on the answer in a misguided attempt to protect her family. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/judges-14.html

**v. 18** ("plowed with my heifer")
- **Most say it simply means "you used my wife."** Gill, Wesley, Benson and Ellicott all take it this way. Gill notes the text says "with" the heifer, not "the heifer." Ellicott sees no good reason to read adultery into it. (The page tags Wesley and Benson as Wesleyan/Methodist and Ellicott as Anglican.) https://www.studylight.org/commentary/judges/14-18.html
- **The adultery reading:**
  - Adam Clarke (tagged Wesleyan/Methodist) reads it as her unfaithfulness. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/judges/14-18.html
  - Haydock (Catholic) allows that reading as possible. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/judges/14-18.html
- Other angles:
  - Constable quotes Lindsey: calling her a heifer mocked her stubborn spirit. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/judges-14.html
  - Henry applies it to Satan working through our own corrupt nature. He also notes Samson paid the wager even though the terms were arguably broken. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jdg/Jdg_014.cfm
- **Catholic reading:** Ambrose treats the answer as a divine mystery, in which danger is turned to safety and bitterness to sweetness. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/34022.htm

**v. 19** (the Spirit and revenge)
- **Not revenge:**
  - Guzik says the Spirit didn't come to soothe a husband's hurt feelings but to serve God's purpose from v. 4. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-14/
  - Keil & Delitzsch say Samson wasn't driven by carnal revenge, and his anger came only after the deed. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/judges/14-19.htm
- **Holy war done with the wrong motives:** Constable calls it an act of holy war that Samson carried out with carnal vengeance, doing God's will for the wrong reason. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/judges-14.html
- **Moral unease:**
  - The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary calls it killing in cold blood, of men who had done him no harm. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/judges/14-14.html
  - Ellicott says the act can only be judged by the standards of its time. https://biblehub.com/judges/14-19.htm
- **Which Ashkelon?** The Cambridge Bible suggests a nearby site rather than the coastal city 24 miles away. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/judges/14-19.htm

**v. 20**
- Constable quotes Keil & Delitzsch: instead of calming Samson, the bride's family made the break permanent. Samson lost his bet, his wife and his honour. His root problem was refusing God's authority. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/judges-14.html
- Haydock (Catholic) suggests her father thought Samson had abandoned her. https://studylight.org/commentaries/hcc/judges-14.html

**Catholic readings of the whole chapter**
- Haydock cites Augustine, who applies the story to Christ building the church of the Gentiles. He also gives a moral reading: sweetness comes from slaying the "lions" of our passions. https://studylight.org/commentaries/hcc/judges-14.html
- Ambrose reads the lion's honey as the Gentiles who believed. https://ccel.org/ccel/schaff/npnf210.iv.ii.iii.i.html
